  "text": "The laundrette clock had stopped at ten past four. Each morning, June checked her watch before switching on the lights.

A man in a brown coat came on Thursdays with a pillowcase full of washing. He separated everything on the folding table, even the socks.

One week he brought a yellow cardigan.

“Low heat?” he asked.

June felt the sleeve between her fingers.

“I’d let that dry on a towel.”

He put it back in the pillowcase.

While his shirts turned behind the glass, he sat beneath the clock and read the instructions on a packet of washing powder.

The following Thursday, he brought the cardigan again.

“It’s gone rather wide.”

“That happens.”

“Can it be made narrow?”

“Not reliably.”

He folded it carefully, matching the cuffs.

In February, the machine nearest the window began leaving water on the floor. June laid down old towels and taped a notice over the coin slot.

The man read it.

“I used to mend these.”

He crouched, then stood with one hand on the folding table.

“Used to,” he said.

She brought him a chair.

He told her which part to ask for. She wrote it on the back of an electricity bill.

After the repair, she offered him a free wash.

He shook his head, but accepted tea.

In April, he arrived carrying a small cloth bag instead of the pillowcase.

June cleared a place on the table.

“Just shirts today?”

“And this.”

He took out the yellow cardigan. Someone had sewn new buttons down the front.

“My granddaughter wears it loose,” he said.

June turned the dryer setting down, then remembered.

“I’ve got a towel somewhere.”"
